result.summary: While the Trojans sleep off their feast, Sinon signals the fleet and the Greeks leave the Wooden Horse, and the city is sacked with fire and slaughter. Priam, Astyanax and many others die, Andromache is enslaved, Aeneas escapes carrying his father and son, Menelaus is disarmed by Aphrodite, and Aethra is reunited with her grandsons.

scenes.title: Drunken feast and Sinon's signal
scenes.summary: The Trojans feast and fall into drunken sleep. Sinon raises a torch, the fleet sails back from Tenedos, and he calls to the men in the Horse.
scenes.stakes: Sinon risks discovery and the failure of the whole plot if a Trojan sees the torch.

scenes.title: The Greeks leave the Horse
scenes.summary: Odysseus and Epeius open the Horse and the chiefs pour out like a wolf and wasps. They kill the guards and set fires.
scenes.stakes: The Greek chiefs risk being caught if any Trojan is still awake.

scenes.title: The fleet returns
scenes.summary: The ships cross from Tenedos with Thetis's help, land at the Hellespont and march silently to Troy to join their comrades.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks inside the city risk being overwhelmed before help arrives.

scenes.title: Night of slaughter
scenes.summary: The Greeks storm through Troy, killing sleeping and drunken Trojans, who also fight back desperately.
scenes.stakes: Trojans face death and the Greeks face a desperate defence.

scenes.title: Deaths of Priam and others
scenes.summary: Diomedes kills Coroebus and Ilioneus, other chiefs kill many, and Achilles' son beheads Priam at the altar.
scenes.stakes: Priam faces death and the end of his house.

scenes.title: Astyanax dies; Andromache enslaved
scenes.summary: The Greeks hurl Astyanax from the tower and drag Andromache into slavery despite her pleas for death.
scenes.stakes: Andromache loses her child and her freedom.

scenes.title: Aeneas escapes
scenes.summary: Antenor's house is spared. Aeneas carries his father and leads his son out, guided by Cypris, and Calchas forbids the Greeks to harm him.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas risks death for himself and his family amid fire and spears.

scenes.title: Menelaus and Helen
scenes.summary: Menelaus kills Deiphobus, finds Helen, and is disarmed by Aphrodite. His brother persuades him to spare her.
scenes.stakes: Helen risks being killed by her husband.

scenes.title: Troy burns
scenes.summary: Ajax son of Oileus outrages Cassandra in Athena's temple while gods mourn. Fire consumes Troy and is seen from far away.
scenes.stakes: The whole city and its people are being destroyed.

scenes.title: Aethra found; Laodice and Electra vanish
scenes.summary: Demophoon and Acamas find their grandmother Aethra and take her to safety. Laodice is swallowed by the earth and Electra hides herself.
scenes.stakes: Aethra risks capture as a Trojan; Laodice faces slavery.

alias_notes.explanation: Cypris is a title of Aphrodite, linked to Cyprus.
Tritonis and Trito-born are epithets of Athena.
Alternative name of Paris, Helen's Trojan abductor.

notable_quotes.reason: Diomedes' chilling reply refusing mercy to the aged Ilioneus.
Calchas praises Aeneas' loyalty to his father and child.
Distant sailors reflect on Fate raising and lowering the great.

analysis.text: The sack shows war's brutality on both sides, with fate and divine will overriding human hopes, and the gods powerless to save Troy.
The poem, by Quintus of Smyrna, retells the epic cycle for a Roman-era audience and links Aeneas' survival to Rome's later greatness.

legacy.text: Aeneas carrying Anchises out of burning Troy became a famous image, central to Virgil's Aeneid and much later art.

fun_facts.text: Quintus of Smyrna wrote the Posthomerica probably in the 3rd or 4th century AD, and it was largely forgotten until its rediscovery in the 15th century.

language_notes.text: "Fluctuant" means wavering or drifting; the drunkards' eyes roll unsteadily.
"Danaans" is a name for the Greeks, after their ancestor Danaus; "naught" means nothing.
"Fulfilled of wine and meat" means filled full with wine and food.
"Achaea's chiefs" are the Greek leaders hidden inside the wooden Horse.
Odysseus is the Greek hero (Ulysses in Latin); this translation uses the Greek form here. He was famed for cunning, hence "subtlety."
"Descry" means to catch sight of; "haply" means perchance. He is checking whether any Trojan is still awake.
"War-fain lords of Hellas' League" means the chieftains eager for battle, of the Greek alliance; Hellas is Greece.
"Achaean" is another name for Greek; Danaans and Argives are used the same way in this passage.
"Those mighty chiefs with foes begirt" means the leaders from the Horse, who are surrounded by enemies.
Enyo is a Greek goddess of war who accompanies Ares in battle and delights in carnage.
"Zeus's bird" is the eagle; "robe and zone" are outer garment and belt, which the women had no time to put on.
"The Fire-god" is Hephaestus, used for fire itself. The feast's roasting spits become weapons.
"Life-ways of man's meat and drink" is a periphrasis for the stomach or gut, where food and drink travel.
"Vaunted" means boasted; "burg" is a fortified town, here Troy.
"Elder of days" means very old, advanced in years.
"Palsied" means paralysed or shaking uncontrollably.
"Suppliant hands" refers to the hands of one begging for mercy; clasping the knees was the formal gesture of supplication.
"While my Strength yet waxeth" means while my strength is still growing or at its height.
Priam is at the altar of Zeus the Hearth-lord, protector of the household, where killing a suppliant was sacrilege.
Priam recalls going to Achilles to ransom the body of his son Hector, whom Achilles had killed, as told in the Iliad.
The Fates were imagined as spinning each person's thread of life, which they cut at the appointed time.
Danaan is another name for the Greeks, from Danaus, a legendary king of Argos. Car-lords means lords who fight from chariots.
Seed means offspring or descendants; here Hector's son.
Dam is the mother animal; haled means dragged by force; thralls are slaves.
Argives is another name for the Greeks, from the city Argos.
Peleus' son is Achilles. He sacked Thebe, Andromache's home city, and killed her father Eetion before he killed Hector.
Spear-thralls are women captured in war and enslaved as prizes of the spear.
Antenor had sheltered Menelaus and Odysseus when they came to Troy to demand Helen back; this is the 'hospitality's debt' the Argives repay.
Themis is the goddess of divine law and right order; she presided over the protection owed to guests and hosts.
Forspent means utterly exhausted; 'lading' is the ship's cargo.
Cypris is a name for Aphrodite, from her cult on Cyprus. She is Aeneas' mother.
'The Fire-god's breath' means the blast of the flames; Hephaestus stands for fire itself (metonymy).
Calchas predicts Aeneas' journey from Troy (by the river Xanthus) to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome on the Tiber.
'It is meet we hold our hands' means it is right that we refrain from attacking him.
"Bower" means a private chamber, here Helen's room. "Ill-starred" means doomed or unlucky.
"Dog" is a harsh insult, implying shamelessness; Homeric heroes use it of those who offend against honour.
"Vaunt thyself Spouse of the child of Zeus" means boast of being husband of Helen, daughter of Zeus. Deiphobus married her after Paris died.
Alexander is another name for Paris, who carried off Helen and was already dead by this point.
Themis is the goddess of divine law and right order. She is pictured watching over human wrongdoing, aided by Zeus.
"Holpen" is an archaic past participle of "help": helped by Zeus.
The Trojans' outrages: Paris stole Helen, broke the oaths sworn over a truce, and violated a sacrifice. Hospitality, oaths and sacrifice were protected by the gods.
"Vengeance-friends" renders the Erinyes or Furies, spirits who punish crimes, especially against oaths and kin.
"Rede" is archaic for counsel or advice.
Tritonis and Trito-born are epithets of Athena (Athene), said to be born by Lake Triton; here the translation also uses Hera for Juno.
"Fane" means temple; "Oileus son" is Ajax the lesser, distinct from Ajax son of Telamon.
"Wreaked" means inflicted; "mortal sufferance" means deadly suffering. The vengeance is Ajax's later death at sea on his voyage home.
"Hearth-lord" refers to Zeus Herkeios, protector of the household altar; Pergamus is Troy's citadel.
"Giving at once in death and tomb" means the burning houses served as both killer and grave.
Ida, Tenedos and Samos are named as places from which the glow could be seen; Tenedos is the island where the Greek fleet hid.
The "Altar" is a southern constellation whose rising was linked to storms; Arcturus is a bright star also associated with stormy weather.
"Staked nets" pictures hunters' nets set around prey, meaning Fate has trapped the Trojans.
"Weened" means supposed or believed; "hale" means drag or haul by force.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe" or "I am sure."
Refers to the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, who attacked Aphidnae to recover their sister Helen, whom Theseus had carried off. Aethra was taken captive then and became Helen's slave.
"Happy mourning's music-beating wings" describes the home resounding with joyful weeping, as if sound beat like wings.
Electra, one of the Pleiades, is said to have hidden herself from grief at Troy's fall; the Pleiades are sometimes counted as only six visible stars.

context_notes.text: Sinon was the Greek who pretended to be a deserter so the Trojans would take the Horse inside the city.
Tenedos is an island near Troy where the Greek fleet had hidden, pretending to sail home.
Epeius built the wooden Horse. The Greeks hid inside it while the Trojans, believing it an offering, brought it into the city.
Thetis is a sea goddess, mother of Achilles, so she favours the Greek fleet.
The Greek fleet had hidden at Tenedos, an island near Troy, pretending to sail home.
The Fates were goddesses who determined the span and death of every life.
Cassandra was Priam's daughter, a prophetess doomed never to be believed. Coroebus was said to have come to Troy hoping to marry her.
Diomedes, son of Tydeus, is one of the great Greek warriors; Hades is the god and realm of the dead.
Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, who joined the Greeks after his father's death and is fierce in the sack of Troy.
Astyanax was the infant son of Hector and Andromache. In this version of the sack of Troy, the Greeks kill him to end Hector's line.
Andromache lost her father Eetion, her husband Hector and now her son, all to Greek violence.
Aeneas is the son of Anchises and Aphrodite, a Trojan hero fated to survive the city's fall.
Calchas is the Greek seer who guided the Greeks with prophecy throughout the war.
Deiphobus, a son of Priam, took Helen as wife after Paris died. Menelaus is Helen's original husband, a Greek king.
Aphrodite, goddess of love, favoured Helen and Paris. Here she protects Helen by overpowering Menelaus's anger with desire.
The speaker is Menelaus's brother Agamemnon, leader of the Greek army, who wants the war's purpose, Helen's recovery, preserved.
Hera and Athena sided with the Greeks throughout the war, so they alone did not mourn.
Ajax dragged Cassandra from Athena's statue, which she clung to; the sacrilege later brought divine punishment on the Greeks.
Helen's abduction by Paris caused the war, so Helen is named as its cause.
Demophoon and Acamas are sons of Theseus, fighting with the Greeks. Aethra is Theseus' mother, so she is their grandmother.
Laodice was a daughter of Priam. In this tradition the earth swallows her to spare her from slavery.
Dardanus, son of Zeus and Electra, was the ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so Electra mourns the fall of her son's city.

literary_notes.text: The swaying, whirling room conveys drunken dizziness through the senses.
The reader knows the Greeks are returning, while the boasting Trojan mocks them and misses the coming doom at his door.
"Their last sleep" signals that many Trojans will die before waking.
Odysseus restrains the eager men, showing his patience and cunning against their battle-lust.
Odysseus slipping from the Horse is compared to a wolf entering a fold, stressing his stealth and predatory hunger.
The Greeks are compared to quiet, harmless sheep, though they march to kill; this contrasts with the earlier wolf image.
The women's cries are like cranes screaming at an eagle, showing helpless terror before a stronger predator.
The Fates gloat over the dead, giving destiny a cruel, watching presence.
The Trojans are slaughtered like swine at a king's feast, making their deaths seem casual and brutal.
The wolves and jackals killing unguarded sheep for sheer lust of slaughter mirror the Greeks and the absent protector, Priam's defenders.
The narrator's exclamation "Ah fool!" breaks in with pity and judgment on Coroebus' empty boasting.
The old man's trembling, with one hand on the sword and one on the knees, shows his terror and desperate pleading.
Death's black doom "stalks" at Neoptolemus' side like a companion, showing his lethal power.
Priam's beheading is compared to a reaper cutting an ear of corn, making the killing seem easy and the old king frail.
The narrator steps in with a mournful reflection on how swiftly human glory is overturned.
Calling the child a wordless babe that knew nothing of war stresses his innocence and sharpens the cruelty of the act.
The extended comparison of a calf driven off a cliff and its mother then seized by lions mirrors Andromache's child-loss and her own enslavement.
The narrator comments on honor and shame, explaining why death seems better to Andromache than slavery.
Aeneas abandoning Troy is compared to a exhausted helmsman leaving a sinking ship for a small boat, conveying hopelessness and the necessity of flight.
The tender child with tears streaming and the old man carried on shoulders evoke pity and show Aeneas' devotion.
Flames parting before Aeneas shows the gods protecting him, marking him as chosen.
Calchas' prophecy of Aeneas' descendants ruling from east to west looks ahead to Roman power.
Themis is described as watching, floating through the air and punishing, making abstract justice an active, ever-present being.
Anger becomes a dark cloud swept away and love becomes deep wells being stirred, turning an emotional change into natural imagery.
Menelaus's frozen stance is compared to a dead tree stump unmoved by any wind, stressing how completely Helen's beauty has paralysed him.
Menelaus appears to rush at Helen but only pretends, so as to hide his softened heart from the Greeks watching.
The goddess cloaks herself in shame and the temple itself groans and quakes, showing the sacrilege through nature's and divinity's reactions.
Repeated "round" and "here... yonder" build the sense of fire spreading everywhere.
The man drowsy with wine, fetching water to quench the flames, is killed by the enemy he thought far away.
The red glare "spread its wings" makes the fire a great bird covering the sky.
The sailors' reflection that Fate raises and lowers men frames Troy's fall as inevitable and beyond the gods' help.
The Greeks' ravaging is compared to winds raging on a storm-tossed sea, an extended epic simile.
A forest fire driving the animals is paired with the Trojans' ruin, stressing helplessness.
A man long thought dead returns home and his family weeps with joy, matching the tearful reunion of Aethra and her grandsons.
Even Zeus must bow to Fate, stressing that Troy's fall is beyond divine power to prevent.
Strife is made a being who controls battle's outcomes, giving the violence a sense of divine agency.
